cards.title: The DM's agenda and principles
cards.body: ### 12.1 The DM's agenda and principles

cards.title: The agenda
cards.body:
**12.1.1 The agenda.** `[N]` At every moment the DM is trying to do three things, in this priority when
they pull apart (subordinate to 00.1.5's precedence of concerns): **(1) portray a world that is true to
its state** — honest, consistent, indifferent to what would be convenient, with its own people pursuing
their own wants; **(2) fill the character's life with adventure** — something to want, something in the
way, something at stake, in every scene; **(3) play to find out what happens** — prepare situations, not
outcomes; let dice, tables and the player's choices decide [R: https://www.dungeonworldsrd.com/gamemastering/
(agenda); R: https://github.com/amazingrando/blades-in-the-dark-srd-content/blob/main/Blades-in-the-Dark-SRD.md
("play to find out what happens"); R6 B-12 ("don't prep plots")].

cards.title: The principles, each with its test
cards.body:
**12.1.2 The principles, each with its test.** `[N]` Each principle is paired with the rule that makes it
checkable; a principle with no rule behind it would be advice the DM forgets by turn eight (R4 W12).

| # | Principle | What it means here | The rule that enforces it |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | **Be a fan of the character** | Want the PC to do remarkable things; never be their enemy — the world is dangerous enough | 12.9 (rotation gives every facet its moment); 12.14.9 (open prompts) |
| P2 | **Address the character, never the player** | Fiction speaks to "you" the character; the player is addressed only in the OOF layer | 12.14.1 |
| P3 | **Begin and end with the fiction** | A ruling is framed in fiction, resolved in state, and returned to fiction | PR-12-1 T4→T9 |
| P4 | **Never speak the name of the rule in the fiction** | No mechanic is voiced by the world; numbers live in OOF blocks | 12.14.4–12.14.5 |
| P5 | **Name every person; give every creature life** | Every NPC has a name, a want and a voice once they matter | 12.11.1–12.11.4 |
| P6 | **Think offscreen too** | The world moves when the PC is not looking — by clocks and the World Turn, never by whim | 12.6.5, ch.11 World Turn |
| P7 | **Draw maps, leave blanks** | Unestablished is not "decided later by taste"; it is settled by the Oracle when first needed | 12.6.1; 00.6.6 |
| P8 | **Say yes to premises; gate capabilities** | "Yes, and" for fictional approaches; Principle VII for what may be attempted | 01.3.9 |
| P9 | **Every refusal leaves a path** | No bare "you can't"; every no names what is possible | 01.3.6; 12.8 |
| P10 | **Present the world honestly** | Odds shown before the die; stakes honored exactly; no fudging | 01.7; 12.7.6 |
| P11 | **Situations, not plots** | Threads have timelines that run if ignored; the PC chooses where to push | ch.11; 12.4.3 |
| P12 | **Know the player** | Ask what they want more and less of; do not infer from silence | 12.5.9 |

[R: https://www.dungeonworldsrd.com/gamemastering/; R5 DM-01, DM-10; R1 12.C; R4 §9 ch.12]

cards.title: What the DM never does
cards.body:
**12.1.3 What the DM never does.** `[D]` [DL-12-01; C:I; R5 DM-01; revision: I-065] A closed list; each is a breach logged with `review_flag` when
detected (12.12.4): (a) choose a number (INV-3); (b) "pick at random" (INV-4); (c) narrate a state change
no tool wrote (INV-1, INV-2); (d) change a committed frame (01.7.2); (e) add a complication outside
01.11.3's list; (f) put a sealed fact in narration (INV-10); (g) speak or decide for the PC beyond the
player's words (12.14.3); (h) voice a mechanic in the fiction (T-00-22); (i) treat a player's assertion
as fact (INV-9); (j) silently skip a registered handler or a fired trigger (INV-15; 12.2.3).

cards.title: The turn loop
cards.body: ### 12.2 The turn loop

cards.title: What a turn is
cards.body:
**12.2.1 What a turn is.** `[D]` [DL-12-01; R5 DM-02; revision: I-065] A **turn** (in this chapter: a *DM turn*, distinct from ch.06's combat
turn) is one player message and the one DM response it produces. The loop of PR-12-1 runs once per
player message. A DM turn may resolve up to three beats (01.2.3), may run world responses (adversary and
NPC actions, triggered events, boundaries), and ends either with narration and an open prompt, or at a
**pause point** (12.2.6) waiting for the player's choice. Session boundaries never advance fictional time
(00.7.9).

cards.title: Classifying the player's message
cards.trigger: every player message (PR-12-1 step T2)
decisions: 1. [J:enum] The message's parts, each classified (a message may hold several): SAFETY — invokes a line, veil, flag or the adjust move, or says content is not okay ("stop", "skip this", "not that", "X-card"). True only when the player signals discomfort with content, not with an outcome. False for "that's unfair" about a result (→ DISPUTE). SESSION — a session move: begin, recap, end, take a break, set a flag, check-in answer, rewind request (12.5). DISPUTE — says the DM made an error ("you said the door was open", "I had two torches", "that's wrong", "she already told me her name"; a message that starts `/fix` is a DISPUTE by code [revision: R2-G]; so is a question why a ruling came out as it did when it implies the result was wrong, "why didn't the success give me the purse?", category `ruling_question` [revision: R2-H]) (→ 12.3.6; a dispute about a deed's ledger line → PR-03-4 [integration: IR ch.03 to 12]). OOF_QUESTION — a rules, codex, odds or "what would it take?" question, or "how was this ruled before?" (no fictional time). PENDING_ANSWER — answers a pause point (commit / change / withdraw at an OFFER; near-miss choice; a ranking; the clarifying question; a redirect choice; a last-chance or recognition choice). FICTION_QUESTION — asks about the world in character or about what the character perceives or knows (G0, 01.3.8). DECLARATION — the character acts (one or more beats, 01.2), including speech meant to change someone's mind (a Talk beat). SPEECH — in-character words that do not try to change someone's mind against their inclination (a free activity, 00.12.6): greetings, answers, small talk, plain questions. Whether an NPC answers a plain question is the NPC's decision (12.2.9). A question is plain, so SPEECH, unless its words request an act or an object or carry pressure (a threat, an offer, a plea, insistence); the listener's wariness does not make it a request [revision: R2-G; I-172]. A step, posture or gesture that only accompanies an act or words is part of it (00.12.6) [I-171]. Default when uncertain between SPEECH and DECLARATION: DECLARATION (SG-05: the roll test then decides). Uncertain between DISPUTE and OOF_QUESTION: OOF_QUESTION answered from the turn log, which surfaces any real error; a fiction part that may also be a dispute is fiction, and the response ends with the fix hint (12.3.6) [revision: R2-G]. A DECLARATION whose computed social DC is certain (15.3.10; T-15-3: a Neutral or warmer listener asked an R1 question) resolves without a roll [revision: R2-C].
2. [D] Order of handling: SAFETY → SESSION → DISPUTE → PENDING_ANSWER → OOF_QUESTION → FICTION_QUESTION → DECLARATION / SPEECH (in the player's order).

3. [J:enum] Beat decisions [revision: R2-C] [DL-12-50]. For each DECLARATION or FICTION_QUESTION part, PARSE (01.2) records only: verb — one of the 15 basic verbs (data/basic_verbs.yaml); target — scene entity ids (01.2.5), or an unnamed description of people or things present ("the refugees", "the queue"; 01.2.7) [revision: R2-I; DL-12-97]; three method facets, yes or no: against_will (acts on a person's body or property against their will; with no will stated, true when the act takes, restrains, moves or harms a person or what they hold without evident consent, false for contact that leaves them free, a tap or a guiding touch [revision: R2-G; I-174]); uses_power (needs a supernatural or licensed technique); speech (mainly words); question_kind (each question part has its own [revision: R2-G; I-173]: an imperative demand for information, "State your name", is a question part; a phatic check, "Can you hear me?", is not; a declared Recall or Observe is a beat, not a question part), one of six: who is X · where is X · what happened · what is X like or for · what do you want or think · who would know; plus topic (the entity asked about, else one of the closed topics of social.yaml#common_knowledge.topics [revision: R2-D]); shape — now, queued (a Ready beat, 01.14.4: "I attack if they keep stalling"), conditional on another beat, or extended (an intent no single attempt achieves, 01.2.2, resolved by a clock, 01.14.6) [revision: R2-G; I-160b]; change — the typed intended change (01.2.7): one kind of resolution.yaml#intended_change.kinds and its slot ids from scope; two changes are two beats [revision: R2-H; DL-01-34]; rests_on — the id of a `said` record in the view when the part acts on what a character said (PR-12-12), else none [revision: R2-H; DL-12-91]. Nothing else is proposed. The gate class, the license and the would-be license (00.12.3, PR-01-5), the roll test (01.4.1) and the DC (01.6.4) are computed by the engine; the PC's knacks reach PARSE as words, never as gates.
cards.computation: the classification is logged with the verbatim message (12.2.5)
state_writes: turn log entry {turn, message verbatim, parts, classes}
narration_may_not_imply: that SPEECH was a persuasion attempt (no roll was made)
cards.worst_case: a SPEECH part classified DECLARATION → a roll test that answers "no roll" (no effect) or an OFFER the player can withdraw for free (class ii); a DECLARATION classified SPEECH → the persuasion attempt is not resolved; the NPC's response comes from its reaction/action table (12.11.5) and the player may declare the attempt next turn (class iv). A SAFETY part missed → caught at T10's safety screen of the draft (12.5.6) [editor: E2-032], which is [D] against the lines list. A wrong verb or facet puts the beat under the wrong card: the OFFER names the act in plain words and the player changes it for free (class ii); a conditional read as "now" is shown in the OFFER before anything is spent (class ii).
examples: inside SPEECH: "'Evening. Is this the ferry?'" (a question asked aloud; also a FICTION_QUESTION if the answer is unestablished). outside (DECLARATION): "'You'll take me across tonight — I'll make it worth your while,'" (tries to change the ferryman's mind: Talk). inside SAFETY: "can we not do the thing with the rats". outside (DISPUTE): "wait, the rats already ran off last turn". non-example: classifying "I search the desk — there's obviously a hidden drawer" as SAFETY or OOF: it is a DECLARATION (Observe) plus an assertion that creates nothing (SG-06).

cards.title: Triggers are loaded, not remembered
cards.body:
**12.2.3 Triggers are loaded, not remembered.** `[T]` + `[D]` At step T3 of every turn the DM calls
`get_active_triggers()` (00.14.2 tool 30), which returns every `[T]` currently true with the rule cards
to load. A fired trigger is handled in the turn it is returned, in this order: (1) safety flags raised
by state (a flagged topic present in the scene, 12.5.6); (2) interrupts from `advance_time` (00.7.8);
(3) lethal-warning and harm-state triggers (ch.07); (4) clock completions and stage changes (00.8.4);
(5) `trg.lead_injection` (12.8.2); (6) recognition and standing offers due (ch.04); (7) pacing-director
pushes due (12.7.4); (8) every other chapter trigger in rule-id order. A trigger may not be deferred to
"a better moment" unless its own rule allows deferral (for example a recognition offer, ch.04). *Worst
case:* none — this is engine-raised; a skipped trigger is breach (j) of 12.1.3 and is detected by the
scene-end sweep (12.4.8 step 4) [R4 SG-11, W12, W13].

cards.title: The packet: what the narrator sees in one turn
cards.body:
**12.2.4 The packet: what the narrator sees in one turn.** `[D]` The DM never works from the whole
ruleset or the whole history. Each turn it receives exactly:
1. **The always-loaded core** (00.15.4): the turn-loop checklist T-12-1 (this chapter's card, about 250
   words), the invariants T-00-1, the gate classes (00.12.3), the stakes/reach/lever card (00.3.9,
   00.3.14–15). It is the same on every call, so it is the packet's cacheable prefix; the active-trigger
   list heads the view instead (item 3) [revision: R2-A].
2. **Loaded rule cards**: by the scene's `situation.*` tags and time mode (12.4.5), by the anchors the
   ANCHOR step retrieves (00.15.3), by fired triggers (12.2.3), and by the PC's held abilities whose
   situation tags match (an ability's card is its data entry; the rank's `text` is quoted verbatim, 05.3.6) [revision: I-030]. Cap: the core plus at most **twelve**
   cards; if more are eligible, triggers first, then anchors, then situation cards by specificity
   (`data/pacing.yaml#packet`). The packet lists the chosen cards from stable to volatile: situation and
   mode cards, then trigger cards, then anchor, precedent and ability cards, so consecutive calls share
   the longest identical prefix for prompt caching [revision: R2-A]. Irrelevant-but-plausible rules degrade accuracy far more than filler
   [R4 W13; R: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08972].
3. **The narrator view of state** (`get_state(scene, narrator)`), headed by the active-trigger list from
   T3: the scene header (the **calendar line** first, pinned and outside every budget: day, month, season, watch and
   weather, 12.16.15 [revision: R2-H; DL-12-95]; then time, mode, place, present entities and their positions, open clocks visible
   to the PC, the scene's agenda), the PC sheet, the present NPCs' records with their active memories of
   the PC (12.11.7), open threads and the cast list, and the permitted slices of anything sealed
   (00.6.5). Nothing sealed is in it (INV-10). Each section has a **token budget**, not an item count
   (`pacing.yaml#packet.view_budget`), so the view does not grow with the game [revision: R2-A]:
   - **Pinned** (always shown, within their own budget): the identity fields, conditions and quantities
     of everyone and everything in view; the written words on things in view; every open commitment
     (each involves the PC, 15.7.6); the present NPCs' active memories (never the archived ones); the
     open pause. A thing with written words stays in view however much else lies at the place.
   - **People present** (the `cast` budget) [revision: R2-A2]: full records for the PC, then the beat's
     target and anyone the message names, then those the PC dealt with most recently, then by 12.6.6
     weight; everyone else present is named on one compact `also here:` line (name and role, within
     `cast_line`, then "and N more"), so a home base that gathers residents does not grow the view and
     nobody present drops out of sight. The pins too are capped: by kind (written words, commitments,
     memories), then newest.
   - **Profiles** [revision: R2-E; DL-12-70]: each person and thing in view, and each spotlight entity, is
     rendered as a compact profile: its stable identity, then its active details (00.6.6a) by salience then last
     use, each marked `(used last turn)` when the previous delivery stated it (12.14.11). `scene` details are
     pinned while their scene runs.
   - **Spotlight** (the `spotlight` budget) [revision: R2-E; DL-12-74]: up to `packet.spotlight_k` (**4**)
     entities outside the scene, chosen in this order, skipping any already in view: (1) entities named or
     aliased in the player's message; (2) the beat's target; (3) entities named in the last delivery; (4) the
     scene agenda's thread and its linked entities; (5) one hop of relationship neighbours of those, while room
     remains. Names resolve through an alias index of names, aliases and roles. A spotlight entity is rendered
     **as the PC knows it**: its name or unnamed label (12.10.2), its profile as the PC perceived it, and the PC's
     knowledge records about it; never its world truth, and a sealed entity shows its permitted slice or nothing
     (INV-10). The spotlight is in the claim check's scope, so a claim about an absent person is judged.
   - **Scene cards** (the `scene_cards` budget) [revision: R2-E; DL-12-73]: at most `packet.max_scene_cards`
     (**2**) cards (12.4.8 step 9): the most recent card involving a present or spotlight entity whose scene
     lies outside the verbatim window (item 5), then the next, read through the role's view below.
   - **Ranked** (fills the facts budget): every other fact about what is in view, by **salience**
     (a memory's salience, 3 for a commitment, 2 for a `scene` detail while its scene runs [revision: R2-E], else 1) **+ recency** (2 for this scene, 1 for the last,
     else 0: it decays per scene, not per turn, so a long scene does not push out its own start)
     **+ relevance** (+2 when the fact's subject or value is the beat's target or an entity the player's
     message names, or a spotlight entity [revision: R2-E]) **+ adjacency** (+1 when its subject has a relationship to anyone present or its
     value names someone present). Ties go to the newest.
   - The other things lying at the place, and the open clocks, fill their budgets newest first; open
     threads and the cast list are ordered by their 12.6.6 weights, then newest.
   The selection is made once per turn and each role reads its projection of it (the table below)
   [revision: R2-E]; a schema offers only the facts that role's view shows.
4. **The player's current message, verbatim and complete** — never a paraphrase (12.2.5).
5. **The last four exchanges verbatim** (player message + DM response), and nothing older except
   through state: the chronicle (11), the threads register, the journal of PC knowledge (15), and the
   scene header. A summary is never the source of truth and is never summarized again (00.6.9d).

*Why four.* Instruction drift appears within about eight rounds of conversation and multi-turn
performance falls most where early assumptions persist [R4 W12; R: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10962;
R: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120]; HiAgent's compression cut commitment conflicts but tripled
player-input conflicts [R1 12.D]. Four verbatim exchanges keep the immediate conversational thread (what
was just said, the pronoun just used, the offer just made) while everything older that matters lives in
typed state that cannot drift. The window is a `pacing.yaml` number (`packet.verbatim_exchanges: 4`);
OEQ-12-1 tests 2/4/8. *Runtime capabilities:* RC-RETRIEVE, RC-STORE, RC-SEAL.

**Views per role.** `[D]` [DL-12-75; revision: R2-E] Item 3's selection is made once per turn; each role reads
its own projection of it, respecting the three layers of 12.10.1 (`get_state(scene, role)`):

| Role | Sees | Never sees |
|---|---|---|
| Reader (PARSE) | the message, the last two exchanges, the names and aliases of the scene and spotlight entities, the PC's knacks as words, the open pause | setting prose, profiles, scene cards |
| Framer (rolled beats only) | the beat; the target's and the place's profiles (their details are levers, 12.14.13); positions and conditions; anchor cards; candidate facts filtered by code | the PC sheet (the modifier is computed), the cast list, setting prose |
| World and the NPC layer | world truth for the present NPCs minus seals: motives, memories, knowledge; off-screen clocks; scene cards | usage marks, setting prose |
| Narrator | **the PC-knowledge layer only**: the adjudication record with handles, the setting and seeded looks (on arrival and at scene framing; on later turns of the scene only as optional material marked described, 12.14.11) [revision: R2-I; DL-12-99], profiles with usage marks, the spotlight as the PC knows it, at most 2 scene cards, the calendar line pinned first; the **speaker card** of each NPC the PC asked or addressed this turn (PR-12-10 step 3: willingness, their ordinary knowledge on the topic, public news, their recent `said` records); and the optional material, marked as such (12.14.12) [revision: R2-H; DL-12-90; DL-12-92] | motives, `truth`, sealed content, undelivered case placements, background the PC has not perceived or learned (beyond a speaker card's ordinary knowledge) |
| Checker | the numbered sentences with their declarations in words (12.3.1), compact profiles of the cited, spotlight and created ids | rule cards outside 12.3, setting prose, the narrator's reasoning |
| Director | threads, clocks, cast weights, scene cards | verbatim exchanges beyond the last one |

Sealed content reaches no view except as its permitted slice (INV-10); a leak test on every Narrator packet
checks that no `truth`, motive or sealed string is in it. The narrator cannot cite what its view does not show,
because its `refs` are built from it (12.3.1).

cards.title: Verbatim in, verbatim logged
cards.body:
**12.2.5 Verbatim in, verbatim logged.** `[D]` [DL-12-02; DL-12-01; C:P13; revision: I-065] The player's message is stored verbatim in the turn log
before anything else happens, and the DM's delivered response is stored verbatim after delivery. The turn
log is the evidence for disputes (12.3.6) and corrections (12.3.4), and the source of "what exactly did I
say?" answers. Nothing in the turn log is ever a fact: facts come only from the six sources of 00.6.7.
The turn log is `available` (the player may ask to see any past exchange). *Runtime capability:* RC-LOG
(the `log_turn` tool, 00.14.2 #35) [editor: E2-033].

cards.title: Pause points (closed list)
cards.body:
**12.2.6 Pause points (closed list).** `[D]` The loop stops mid-turn and returns to the player, delivering
everything resolved so far plus one pause message (format 12.15), only at these points:
1. **OFFER awaiting commit** (01.7.1) — unless auto-commit applies (01.7.4).
2. **Clarifying question** (01.2.4) — at most one per declaration.
3. **Redirect awaiting a choice** (01.3.6) — when the player must accept a fallback or choose another way.
4. **Near-miss choice** (01.9.3) — failure, or success at a cost (threatened or alternate).
5. **Ranking request** for a bundled beat (01.10.3) — if the player did not rank at OFFER.
6. **Last-chance menu** (ch.07) and **yield terms** (ch.07).
7. **Recognition or institutional offer** (ch.04, ch.11) — accept / decline / defer.
8. **Generator `chosen` fill** (00.11.3 step 4) — pick one of up to three.
9. **Rewind or correction choice** (12.3.4, 12.5.8).
At a pause point no time passes and no state changes beyond what was already resolved. A pause that the
player does not answer persists: the next message is first checked as a PENDING_ANSWER (12.2.2). If the
next message instead declares something new, an open OFFER is treated as **withdrawn** (nothing spent),
an open near-miss choice defaults to **failure** (01.9.3's default), an open ranking defaults to the
declaration order (01.10.3), and offers from 04/11 stay open under their own rules. *Worst case:* none
(engine defaults) [R7 §4.0 step 6; 01.7.1].

cards.title: Player-input fidelity
cards.worst_case: a missed substitution reaches the player — it is a correction case (12.3.4), and the player's dispute is answered from the turn log (class iv) [R1 #3 (NCP player-input rule: "denial or redirection is fine only when the player's intent is acknowledged and followed through concretely"); R1 T-2].
cards.body:
**12.2.7 Player-input fidelity.** `[J:flag]` ×3 Before delivery (PR-12-1 step T10) the draft is checked for
three properties, each `[J:flag]`, each true only when the named evidence exists in the draft:
1. **Acknowledged** — every DECLARATION, FICTION_QUESTION and SPEECH part of the message is answered in
   the response, in the order given (resolved, queued per 01.2.3, paused, or redirected). Evidence: some
   sentence cites each part's record line (coverage, 12.3.1a) [revision: R2-B; I-150]; a turn with no player
   part (the opening) has nothing to acknowledge.
2. **Not substituted** — no part is resolved as a different action than the player declared (a "search
   the desk" is not resolved as "search the room"; a Talk to persuade is not resolved as an intimidation).
   Evidence: each frame's neutral restatement (01.2.6) matches the player's words, or the stated assumed
   reading (01.2.4) was shown.
3. **Not silently reset** — nothing the player's prior resolved actions established is undone or
   ignored (a door they broke stays broken; the coin they paid is gone; the NPC they insulted remembers).
   Evidence: the claim check (12.3) found no contradiction with this scene's writes.
A false flag sends the draft back to T7 with the failure named. *Worst case (J):* a missed substitution
reaches the player — it is a correction case (12.3.4), and the player's dispute is answered from the turn
log (class iv) [R1 #3 (NCP player-input rule: "denial or redirection is fine only when the player's
intent is acknowledged and followed through concretely"); R1 T-2].

cards.title: Adjudication is written before prose
cards.body:
**12.2.8 Adjudication is written before prose.** `[D]` Steps T4–T6 of PR-12-1 produce an **adjudication
record** for the turn — the frames (00.13), the world responses (12.2.9) with their table rolls and
fortune checks, and the full list of state writes — and every write is made through tools *before* the
narration draft exists. The narration is then written *from* the record and the fresh narrator view, never
the other way round. A thing that "would be cool to narrate" but is not in the record is either sourced
now through a legitimate step (an Oracle question, a table roll, a write-on-mention of a new element)
or left out [R4 R-07, §8; R2 ch.12 "code owns outcomes, narration owns flavor"; 01.12.1].

cards.title: World responses inside a turn
cards.worst_case: an NPC acts from a table where a recorded want applied — one NPC action of ordinary weight, reversible by the next exchange (class iv); the NPC's record is in the packet, so the claim check flags a response contradicting a recorded refusal [R4 W4; R5 P-06].
cards.body:
**12.2.9 World responses inside a turn.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` After the player's beats resolve (and in
conflict, as ch.06's turn order dictates), the world responds in this fixed order, each only from its
closed source (01.11.3):
1. **Adversaries and hostile NPCs in conflict** act on their turns from their behavior priority lists
   (ch.09) by PR-06-6, an adversary's turn [revision: I-030]; their attacks are rolled by the engine against the PC's defenses (00.3.3).
2. **NPCs present** follow the default NPC layer (12.11.9) [revision: R2-B; DL-12-43; I-140; revision: R2-H;
   DL-12-93]. Each NPC's activity is rolled once per scene and is optional material. Only an NPC the PC addressed, or
   whom the event concerns (a matching tag, `social.yaml#event_tags.concerns`), responds, within the scene's
   practice, and the response comes from (a) a resolved Talk frame's delivered outcome (ch.15), or for a question the
   PC asked, PR-12-10 (the case graph for a consequential question; otherwise willingness only, the words being the
   narrator's) [revision: R2-D; DL-12-60; revision: R2-H; DL-12-90], else (b) an established want or refusal whose
   tags match the event's (`social.yaml#event_tags`; 12.11.9 step 3(b)) [revision: R2-G; DL-12-87], else (c)
   `roll_table(tbl.npc_action)` with the NPC's standing as context (12.11.5). **An addressed NPC always answers**, in
   words, or with a refusal spoken in their own voice. An addressed answer and each response deed are record lines the
   narration cites (12.14.12). The DM chooses the *words*; the source decides *whether* and *what is done*.
3. **Clocks** that ticked from this turn's costs, consequences or `auto_ticks` render their omens
   (INV-14), and completions run (00.8, PR-00-3).
4. **Fired triggers** in 12.2.3's order (lead injection, pacing pushes, offers).
5. **Time**: the beat's time cost is applied by its mode (00.7.3); any boundary crossed runs its
   handlers (INV-15); an interrupt halts and frames a new moment (00.7.8).
*Worst case (J, 2c vs 2b):* an NPC acts from a table where a recorded want applied — one NPC action of
ordinary weight, reversible by the next exchange (class iv); the NPC's record is in the packet, so the
claim check flags a response contradicting a recorded refusal [R4 W4; R5 P-06].

cards.title: Read before you narrate
cards.body:
**12.2.10 Read before you narrate.** `[D]` Any quantity, condition, harm state, position, possession,
clock state or standing the narration mentions is read from the narrator view fetched *after* this turn's
writes (step T6), never from memory or from the adjudication record's intermediate values. Models act
correctly on a correctly retrieved updated fact only about 55% of the time; the remedy is to quote the
store [R1 12.D]. Every quantity, condition, position, possession or standing a sentence states cites the fresh
view's id for it in its `refs` (12.3.1), so the read is checkable: a stated value with no such ref is undeclared
(12.3.1a) [revision: R2-B; DL-12-41]. Only a value on 12.3.1b's blocking list (a quantity, a condition, a coarse
position, a relevant possession) blocks; a standing or clock value with no ref is logged [revision: R2-G].

cards.title: The claim check and error correction
cards.body: ### 12.3 The claim check and error correction

cards.title: Claims
cards.worst_case: a claim neither declared nor found by a code scan escapes the check — it is caught later by the scene-end sweep (12.4.8) when it is on the blocking list, or by the player's `/fix` (12.3.6), class iv [revision: R2-G].
cards.body:
**12.3.1 Claims.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` [DL-12-25; DL-12-03; C:P13; R5 DM-08; revision: I-065] A **claim** is any assertion in a draft narration that the store
could confirm or contradict, held as `{subject id, claim class, predicate, value}`. Claims come from two places
[revision: R2-B; DL-12-41]:
1. **The narrator's sentence declarations** (`[J:enum]`). A draft is a list of sentences, and each sentence
   declares `refs` (the handles of this turn's adjudication-record lines, `R1`, `R2`…, and fact ids from the
   narrator view; both lists are built from the packet, so nothing outside the packet can be cited), `about`
   (the ids in scene scope it speaks of), `new` (each new element it introduces, typed by `element_kind`, with
   the properties it states; 12.14.13), an `atmosphere` flag, and a `speaker` id when the sentence, or a quoted
   part of it, is a character's speech (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G]. Code resolves each declaration into claims
   with the subject given, never guessed.
2. **Any undeclared assertion a code scan finds** in a narrator-voice sentence: a numeral, a name or alias, an
   outcome word or a sealed string (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G; DL-12-83]. It is judged now, like a declared claim.
   **The audit is a sampled measurement, never a per-turn gate** [revision: R2-G; DL-12-83]. On **1 turn in 10**
   (picked by the turn id, so it draws nothing from the game's dice; `pacing.yaml#claim_check.audit`), after
   delivery, the Checker reads the numbered sentences, each with its declarations rendered in words, and compact
   profiles of the ids they cite (12.2.4's Checker view), and reports (i) assertions a sentence makes beyond its
   declarations (`[J:flag]` per sentence: *"Does this sentence assert something its declarations do not
   cover?"*) and (ii) declarations the sentence does not express; a full extraction runs on the same turn to
   measure what the diff misses [revision: R2-E; DL-12-71]. Its findings go to the claim log (12.3.1b); they never
   cut, redraft or delay a delivered turn. The blocking checks that can be code run on every turn: numerals
   against quantities, names against the names the PC knows and the sealed strings, outcome words against the
   frame's degree and reach.

The claim classes (closed list) and what each is checked against:

| Class | Examples of claims | Checked against |
|---|---|---|
| `existence` | "a guard stands by the gate"; "the rats are gone" | entity `exists`, scene presence |
| `identity` | a name, sex or pronoun, age, kin, title, profession, species, appearance detail | entity fields, identity facts, and the entity's `lasting` details (`detail.<slot>`, 00.6.6a) [revision: R2-E] |
| `quantity` | "your last two arrows"; "a purse of twelve silver" | quantities |
| `harm_condition` | "you're bleeding"; "he's barely standing"; "you shake off the fear"; "he is dead" | conditions, harm state, shown descriptors (bloodied, down); a death only with `harm_state.dead` (07) [revision: I-030] |
| `position` | "she's at your shoulder"; "she leaves"; "he has you pinned"; a present NPC's continuing activity ("the smith works at her forge") [revision: R2-B; I-128] | position, range bands, positional flags (T-06-4's words, T-12-11) [revision: I-030]; an activity against the NPC's presence and the activity code wrote for the scene (T1c, 12.11.9); a posture, hold, manner or activity against the entity's `scene` details (00.6.6a) [revision: R2-E], judged against its record line (T-12-18) [revision: R2-F]. **Only coarse position is a claim** (owner ruling, DL-12-77): the place someone is in, a range band to the PC, held or pinned or freed, mounted, arriving or leaving. Fine placement within a place ("by the hearth", "leaning on the bar", "crosses to the window") is atmosphere (T0, 12.14.13): never stored, never judged. A place named only by a common noun ("the hall") does not place something that is here elsewhere, since the words may name this place's own part, and a place after a direction word (toward, past, beyond) is a direction, not a location [revision: R2-F] |
| `possession` | "you pocket the key"; "the captain draws his sword" | possessions, equipped |
| `location_time` | "dusk falls"; "two days after the fire"; "in the archive" | time, place graph (temporal claims are computed, 00.6.9e) |
| `knowledge` | "you recognize the seal"; "he knows you're lying"; "you remember her name" | knowledge records (PC and NPC) |
| `capability` | what a license, ability or item does or cannot do | license `scope` at grade (INV-8) |
| `clock` | an omen; "the alarm is spreading"; a completion | clock state, the omen the engine selected |
| `attitude` | "she warms to you"; "he's furious" | standing rung, NPC memory, the frame's delivered reach |
| `outcome` | "you make it across"; "the lock gives"; "it costs you" | the frame's degree, delivered reach, the chosen cost form |
| `action` | a deed that changes something: "the guard steps aside"; "your companion cuts the rope"; "the merchant pockets the coin and leaves" (a continuing activity is `position`) | the act's closed source in this turn's adjudication record (12.2.9): a behavior list, a Talk frame's outcome, a recorded want or refusal, a `tbl.npc_action` row, a clock or trigger; for an ally, one of 16.13.3's six reasons [revision: I-030] |
| `sealed` | anything matching a sealed fact's content | the sealed partition (a match is a leak) |

**Which claims block** is 12.3.1b's closed list; every other claim is judged only to be logged [revision: R2-G].
Declaration is `[J:enum]`: the narrator assigns each assertion of a sentence its refs and class; the audit reads
each sentence's text for what the declarations missed [revision: R2-B].
**`narrated` certainty** [revision: R2-E; DL-12-70]: a fact that narration first stated (a T1a element or detail,
00.6.6a) is written with `certainty: narrated`. It is canon like an established fact: it supports later claims
and contradicts differing ones (whole store, 12.3.2), and only an explaining event in a turn's record supersedes
it. It differs only in provenance, so it never creates value, a clue or a hazard (12.14.13).
**Atmosphere is never a claim** [revision: I-127; DL-12-37]: sensory and ambient detail that names nothing
addressable (weather, light, sky, smell, temperature, a sound with no source the player could approach, the
murmur of an unnamed crowd, mood) is not extracted, matching 00.6.6, which never records it. Such detail is
checked only against `location_time` (season words by a code scan against the calendar line, 12.3.2 [revision: R2-H];
it may not contradict the hour, season, weather or climate the store
holds) and the lines and veils (12.5.6). When it is uncertain whether a phrase is atmosphere or names an
addressable element, it is an element: it is declared, and it is written by its tier (12.14.13)
[revision: R2-B]. *Worst case (J):* a claim neither declared nor found by a code scan escapes the check — it is caught
later by the scene-end sweep (12.4.8) when it is on the blocking list, or by the player's `/fix` (12.3.6), class iv
[revision: R2-G].

cards.title: Sentence coverage
cards.body:
**12.3.1a Sentence coverage.** `[D]` [DL-12-41; R1 12.D; revision: R2-B] Code checks three things about every
draft from its declarations, before any verdict:
1. **Every sentence is declared or atmosphere.** A sentence cites at least one ref, `about` id or `new`
   element, or it carries the atmosphere flag. A sentence with neither is undeclared.
2. **Atmosphere names nothing addressable.** A sentence flagged as atmosphere that contains a name, an alias or
   description of anything in scene scope, a numeral, or a new addressable element (00.6.6) is undeclared. Code
   scans for names, aliases and numerals; the sampled audit (12.3.1) measures the rest [revision: R2-G].
3. **Every must-name item is cited.** Each item 12.14.12 requires this turn is an adjudication-record line with
   a handle, and some sentence's `refs` cites it. An uncited item is a coverage failure of the turn. Optional material (12.14.12) is never a must-name item
   and is never required [revision: R2-H; DL-12-92].

An undeclared sentence, or an atmosphere sentence that names something, is delivered as drafted and logged unless
a code scan finds a blocking-list hit in it (a numeral, an unknown name, an outcome word, a sealed string; 12.3.1b);
only then is it redrafted with declarations, or cut [revision: R2-G; DL-12-80]. An uncited must-name item is
supplied by 12.3.3. Coverage replaces the Checker's judgement that the
record's parts were acknowledged (12.2.7, flag 1). Citing per sentence lets code judge each claim with its
subject given; a second reading that guesses what the prose claimed disagreed with itself on a third of
unchanged sentences in playtest.

cards.title: What blocks: the narrator's voice, a closed list, a certain subject
cards.worst_case: a real error that is off the list, or whose subject is uncertain, reaches the player — a wrong coat colour, an attitude out of step with the record, a walk-on misnamed in passing. Each is incidental by construction (anything mechanical is on the list); the claim log keeps it, and the player's `/fix` corrects it (12.3.6), where an incidental reading the record cannot refute goes the player's way (class iv). Evidence: in 30 live turns every position failure was a checker false positive, and the other failures came from figurative prose, restated leads and labels resolved to the wrong entity (DL-
cards.body:
**12.3.1b What blocks: the narrator's voice, a closed list, a certain subject.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` [DL-12-80;
DL-12-81; DL-12-82; revision: R2-G] The claim check guards what play depends on and lets the rest through. A claim
**blocks** (its verdict's fix in 12.3.2 applies: a redraft or a cut) only when all three hold: it is in the
narrator's voice, its subject is certain, and it is on the blocking list. Every other claim is **logged**: the
sentence is delivered as drafted, a new ordinary element or detail in it is written by its tier (12.14.13), and a
claim-log record `{turn, sentence, class, verdict, store_value}` is kept for review and for disputes (12.3.6).
1. **Narrator voice and speech** `[J:enum]`. Words a character says, quoted or reported with a declared `speaker`
   ("'The ferry left at dawn,' says Maren"; "she tells you it left at dawn"), are **speech**; everything else is
   the narrator's voice. Speech is **testimony**: it is recorded as a `said` record on the speaker `{speaker,
   turn, words, about}`, never as a fact about the world, and it is never checked for truth, for what the speaker
   knows (12.10.6) or for secrets. The narrator never sees sealed content (INV-10), so a "leak" in speech is only a
   claim, and it may be false. Speech is checked for four things only, all by code: the speaker is present in the
   scene, the speaker is not the PC, no words are put in the PC's mouth beyond what the player said
   (`pc_agency`; this covers words given to the PC inside an NPC's speech or its attribution, "'Fair enough,' you
   say": a speaker tag never exempts them [revision: R2-I; DL-12-100]), and the words do not repeat a line the speaker already said (their `said` records, 12.14.11)
   [revision: R2-H; DL-12-90]; season words are scanned in speech too (item 2.7). Speech never unseals anything, never delivers a clue (a clue is delivered only by its placement,
   15.9), and never writes a fact. A name heard in speech that matches the entity's stored name is known to the PC
   from then on (a knowledge record, `how: heard`); any other name stays a said claim. A said claim becomes world
   truth only when it matters (PR-12-12): the player acts on it (they go looking for "old Marta at the mill"), cites
   it as a lever, travels to a place it names, or it would change a mechanical outcome. It is then settled once: by
   the case if consequential, else accepted, or by the Oracle at Likely when it would help or hinder beyond the
   ordinary; a "no" means the speaker was wrong or lied [revision: R2-H; DL-12-91].
2. **The blocking list** (closed; the narrator's voice only):
   1. the **outcome** against the roll's degree and delivered reach, including a license, item or effect
      described doing more than its scope (`outcome`, `capability`; `overreach`);
   2. **harm, conditions and quantities** (`harm_condition`, `quantity`);
   3. **possession of a mechanically relevant item**: a weapon, armour, tool, key, consumable, coin, or an item
      cited as a lever or of more than common value (`possession`); who holds a cup or a pipe is not on it;
   4. **coarse position**: the place, the range band to the PC, held or pinned, mounted, departed (DL-12-77); and
      **presence and alive status** (`position`, `existence`);
   5. **PC agency**: the narration decides what the PC does, says or feels (`pc_agency`, 12.14.3);
   6. **sealed content, or a name the PC does not know**, stated in the narrator's voice (`sealed`; `identity` for
      a name only);
   7. a **precision check's hit** (12.3.2, *Precision, not class*): the pronoun of a certain subject, and a season
      word against the calendar line, in the narrator's voice and in speech alike [revision: R2-H; DL-12-95].
   A change on the list with no write this turn is `unsourced_change` and is cut (an NPC who "pockets the coin and
   leaves" changes a quantity and a position). Owed blocks (12.3.2), must-name coverage (12.3.1a) and the safety
   screen (12.5.6, not a claim check) are unchanged.
3. **Everything else is never cut** `[J:enum]`: descriptive detail, an incidental NPC act (she wipes the bar, he
   laughs), an attitude, an ordinary fact, a new ordinary element. New things are written as established by their
   tier (T1a, 12.14.13), or logged when they cannot be written (no slot, no subject). A clash with a stored
   incidental detail (a coat's colour, a posture, an ordinary property) is logged, not blocked: the store keeps its
   value, and the player may dispute either (12.3.6). **A consequential element (T2) stated in the narrator's
   voice with no source is still cut**: a clue, a culprit, a person with a want or a secret, an adversary, a
   hazard. Its kind is declared, so the cut needs no matching and cannot be a false positive; it is rare; and once
   delivered as world truth it would bend the case graph (15.9), which only generators feed. The same thing said
   in speech is testimony and passes (item 1). Settling is not checking: an unsettled consequential property a
   sentence states (locked, armed, knows) is still settled by the Oracle before it binds (12.3.2 `undetermined`).
4. **A certain subject** `[D]`. A claim takes a verdict, `contradicted` and `supported` alike, only when its
   subject resolves to exactly one entity: (a) a unique proper name or alias; (b) an id declared in the sentence's
   `about` that is the only entity in scope the sentence's words could name (the only sword in the scene, the only
   woman at the bar); (c) the only candidate present. The PC ("you") and this turn's beats are always certain. Not
   certain: a common noun with two or more fitting candidates in scope, even when declared ("the sword is green"
   with a red and a green sword present); a place named by a common noun ("the hall"); a pronoun with two
   antecedents. A claim with no certain subject takes no verdict and is logged; a declared new element in its
   sentence is still written by its tier.
*Worst case (J):* a real error that is off the list, or whose subject is uncertain, reaches the player — a wrong
coat colour, an attitude out of step with the record, a walk-on misnamed in passing. Each is incidental by
construction (anything mechanical is on the list); the claim log keeps it, and the player's `/fix` corrects it
(12.3.6), where an incidental reading the record cannot refute goes the player's way (class iv). Evidence: in 30
live turns every position failure was a checker false positive, and the other failures came from figurative prose,
restated leads and labels resolved to the wrong entity (DL-12-80).

cards.title: Verdicts
cards.body:
**12.3.2 Verdicts.** `[D]` `check_claims(claims)` (00.14.2 tool 32, RC-AUDIT) returns one verdict per
claim (closed list). A verdict's fix applies only when the claim blocks (12.3.1b); any other verdict is logged and
its sentence delivered as drafted [revision: R2-G; DL-12-80]:

| Verdict | Means | Required fix |
|---|---|---|
| `supported` | the narrator packet or this turn's adjudication record holds it (scope below) [revision: R2-B] | none |
| `new_element` | a new addressable element the store does not hold, contradicting nothing | write it by its declared `element_kind`'s tier (12.14.13) [revision: R2-B]: a T1a element is written on mention now (00.6.6) with only the properties the sentence states; a T2 element (a clue, an item beyond common value, a hazard or trap, an adversary, or a person with a want, secret or thread knowledge) not in this turn's record is cut when the narrator's voice states it (or brought in through its owning procedure); said in speech, it is testimony and passes (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G]. An element not written at the draft's write-on-mention step is still written here; an unknown subject is never cut merely for being new [revision: I-127] |
| `undetermined` | a property of an existing element the store has not settled (is the door locked? her pronoun?) | split by tier (12.14.13) [revision: R2-B; DL-12-40; I-132]: **incidental** (an ordinary property of a thing in view, one 12.14.13's question finds false: a coat's colour, a worker's trade, a notice's lettering; T1a) → written on mention as drafted, and it binds later turns; **consequential** (locked, armed, present, knows, or anything the question finds true; uncertain → consequential) → ask the Oracle or roll the table that settles it, write the answer, and redraft that sentence to it. An answer that agrees with the draft passes with no redraft; once answered, the property is settled, so a redraft is `supported` or `contradicted`, never asked again |
| `contradicted` | the store, anywhere (scope below), holds a different value for a certain subject (12.3.1b) | on the blocking list: redraft to the store's value; otherwise logged, and the store keeps its value [revision: R2-G] |
| `unsourced_change` | the draft says something *changed* (a quantity, a condition, a possession, a position, a standing) with no write this turn, or says a non-player entity *acted* with no source in the adjudication record (an `action` claim; an ally's act with none of 16.13.3's reasons) [revision: I-030] | on the blocking list: cut it; an incidental act or change (she sets down her cup, he turns away): logged, never cut and never written as a change [revision: R2-G]; a change is never written to match prose (INV-1) |
| `overreach` | a license, item or effect described doing more than its scope; an outcome beyond the delivered reach; a cost of another entry or severity | redraft to the literal scope / the frame |
| `leak` | the claim matches a sealed fact | in the narrator's voice: cut it; replace with the permitted slice (tell, omen, atmosphere). Speech never leaks: it is testimony (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G] |
| `pc_agency` | the draft gives the PC words, choices, feelings or actions the player did not state and no resolved effect licenses | cut it (12.14.3) |

**Owed blocks.** `[D]` A turn for which `get_active_triggers` returned `trg.lethal_warning` owes a
`[WARNING]` block, and one that returned `trg.exits` owes a `[STATUS]` block (12.15.15, T-07-7). A draft that
lacks an owed block fails the check as if a claim were `contradicted`: it is redrafted with the block, and the
plain fallback (12.3.3) carries it too, since a warning is never omitted (07.3.4) [revision: I-030].

**Support and contradiction scope.** `[D]` [revision: R2-B; DL-12-42; revision: R2-G] Only a claim with a certain
subject (12.3.1b item 4) is judged at all. Support is judged against the narrator packet plus this turn's
adjudication record; contradiction is judged against the whole store, and blocks only on the blocking list
(12.3.1b item 2). A claim that only an
off-packet fact supports passes as `supported` and is logged as a **retrieval miss**, which measures how well the
view was selected (12.2.4). A claim the packet supports but a fact anywhere in the store contradicts is
`contradicted`. A claim nothing supports or contradicts takes its verdict from the table (`new_element`,
`undetermined`, `unsourced_change`).

**Precision, not class, decides blocking.** `[D]` [revision: R2-H; DL-12-95] Whether a check blocks is decided by its
measured precision, not by its claim's class. A cheap code check whose hits are real errors at least
`claim_check.precision_checks.min_precision` (0.95) of the time on the narration gate corpus blocks even when its
class is off the blocking list: its sentence is redrafted to the store's value, as a blocking `contradicted` claim is.
A check measured below that line is logged only, whatever its class; the rate is re-measured each playtest round
(OEQ-12-27). The first two, adopted on the owner's ruling and to be confirmed by measurement:
1. **The pronoun of a certain subject**: a third-person pronoun whose antecedent is certain (12.3.1b item 4: the only
   person named in that sentence or the one before, with no other person of a fitting pronoun between) against the
   subject's stored `gender_pronouns` (12.11.1). An uncertain antecedent stays log-only.
2. **Season words**: a season word or season-bound phrase ("spring", "the autumn harvest", "midwinter") naming a
   season other than the calendar line's (12.2.4, 12.16.15), with no time-shift word in its clause
   (`precision_checks.checks.season_words.time_shift_words`: last, next, ago, coming, since, until …), in the
   narrator's voice or in speech: the season in front of a speaker is the scene's, not testimony about the world
   beyond it.

The **one asymmetry**: a `new_element` may be written to the store because the narration is creating
a new, non-conflicting thing — exactly what write-on-mention exists for — but an `unsourced_change` may
never be, because a change needs a resolved source (a frame, a handler, an effect, an Oracle answer)
[INV-1; 00.6.6; R1 T-14 (tool state wins; "latest wins" only among writes)].

cards.title: Per-sentence repair and the plain fallback
cards.body:
**12.3.3 Per-sentence repair and the plain fallback.** `[D]` [revision: R2-B; DL-12-41; I-131; I-133; I-135; I-136]
A draft is repaired one sentence at a time, each failing sentence by the table's rule (12.3.2). A sentence whose
fix is a cut (a blocking `unsourced_change`; a `leak`, `pc_agency` or a T2 element not in the record, in the
narrator's voice; a sentence a code scan flagged that cites no must-name item) is dropped by code. Any other
blocking failure is redrafted; a sentence whose claims are only logged is never touched (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G]. A **redraft** re-writes
only the failing sentences, each sent with its failure and the store's value to use; sentences that passed,
atmosphere included, are kept as written and are not re-sent or re-checked [revision: I-127; DL-12-37]. A redraft
instruction never asks the narrator to shorten, simplify or play safe. At most **two redrafts**
(`pacing.yaml#claim_check.max_redrafts`).

After the second redraft, a sentence that still fails is cut, and every must-name item (12.14.12) that no
remaining sentence cites is stated by its **rendered line**: one sentence built by code from the record item's
typed fields (a frame's restated beat and its degree in words, the chosen cost form, a visible condition, an
omen, a changed position, an NPC's response, a lead, a FICTION_QUESTION's answer stated as the fact it settled).
A rendered line is always a statement, never a question and answer ("Traders are setting up stalls? Yes." is
never shown). The delivered narration is the passing sentences in their order, each rendered line in the place of
the sentence it replaces, then the OOF blocks and the open prompt (12.14.9), which code restores if it was cut.

The **plain fallback** is this rule when no drafted sentence passes: every must-name item is rendered, with the
scene header only when this turn opened a scene (12.4). A turn that needed any rendered line logs a ruling record
with `kind: rule_conflict`, `review_flag: true`; a turn repaired by cuts alone, with every must-name item still
cited, logs none. A rendered line is dull but true; a vivid falsehood is worse, because every later turn builds
on it [R1 12.D; C:III].

cards.title: Correcting an error the player has already seen
cards.worst_case: an in-fiction reconciliation chosen where it smuggles in a convenient fact — it is visible in the correction record and the claim check of the reconciliation sentence itself catches a new fact (`unsourced_change` or `new_element` verdicts are illegal in a reconciliation), class iv; a reliance flag wrongly false — the player raises it as a DISPUTE and the procedure reruns, class iv [R1 G-3, #2; R4 §3.3 W9; C:III; C:P13].
cards.body:
**12.3.4 Correcting an error the player has already seen.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` When a mismatch between
something already delivered and the store is found — by the scene-end sweep (12.4.8), by a later claim
check, or by the player (12.3.6) — the DM runs PR-12-4:
1. **Find the truth.** *State wins* (INV-2) — with one exception: a **record error**, where the narration
   matched a legitimately resolved outcome but a write it required was missed or mis-entered (the frame
   delivered the key; `set_fact` never ran). Test `[J:flag]`: *"Does a resolved source in the log (a frame,
   a handler result, an Oracle answer, a generator output) require the narrated value?"* True only when
   that source's id can be named. True → the store is repaired by a corrective write citing the source
   (`source: correction`, `supersedes` the wrong value, pinned, 12.3.6) [revision: R2-G]. False → it is a
   **narration error** and the store stands.
2. **Choose the form** `[J:enum]`:
   - **In-fiction reconciliation** — true only when one sentence of fiction can make the delivered
     narration consistent with the store *without creating any new fact that helps or hinders anyone*
     ("You count again: twelve coins, not twenty — the dim light fooled you"). False when the fix would
     need a new event, a new object, a changed NPC mind, or a convenient excuse.
   - **OOF correction note** — format 12.15.9; one or two lines, plain, no apology essay.
   - Default when uncertain: the OOF note. A record error always gets the OOF note (the player should
     know the record was wrong), optionally plus an in-fiction line.
3. **Reliance.** `[J:flag]` *"Did the player, after the error and before this correction, commit any beat
   that cited, targeted or premised the erroneous claim?"* True only when a frame's levers, target,
   method, or the player's words name it. If true:
   - **Within the current scene**: the player chooses (pause point 9) one of: **keep** — offered only
     when the beat's committed frame remains valid with the erroneous element removed (no lever, target
     or premise rested on it); the result stands untouched; **accept forward** — the beat's resolved
     result stands and the false element is corrected around it (for a player who prefers that to
     re-rolling); or **rewind** — the store is restored from the write history to just before that beat
     (`revert_writes`, 00.14.2 #36) [editor: E2-034], the beat's rolls are logged as voided, and the player
     re-declares. A committed roll is never recomputed with different numbers (01.8.5). Rewinds go back at
     most to the turn of the error, and past the current scene's start only under 12.5.8's take-back limit
     [revision: R2-G].
   - **Before the current scene**: no rewind. The correction runs forward, and the player is **made
     whole** for quantities spent *because of* the falsehood: each such spend (coin, Focus, supply, a
     consumable, fate) is restored by a corrective write. Nothing else is compensated (no free success, no
     bonus) — the aim is to remove the error's effect, not to pay damages.
4. **Log** a correction record `{turn_of_error, turn_found, found_by, claim, store_value, kind:
   narration_error|record_error, form, reliance, rewound_beats, refunds}` to the corrections ledger
   (`available`), and a ruling record with `review_flag: true` (12.12.4).
*Worst case (J):* an in-fiction reconciliation chosen where it smuggles in a convenient fact — it is
visible in the correction record and the claim check of the reconciliation sentence itself catches a new
fact (`unsourced_change` or `new_element` verdicts are illegal in a reconciliation), class iv; a reliance
flag wrongly false — the player raises it as a DISPUTE and the procedure reruns, class iv
[R1 G-3, #2; R4 §3.3 W9; C:III; C:P13].

cards.title: What is never corrected away
cards.body:
**12.3.5 What is never corrected away.** `[D]` [DL-12-04; C:P8; revision: I-065] A correction never: re-rolls a die whose frame was valid;
changes a degree, a delivered reach or a cost that was correctly resolved; removes a consequence the
player's own declared method caused; or rewinds past a lethal frame's resolution, a recognition grant
the player accepted, or a session boundary. Those are outcomes, not errors (01.8.5).

cards.title: Disputes: the player's report
cards.worst_case: a valid report rejected — it stays in the review log with the player's words and the evidence, and the player can report it again with the turn (class iv); an incidental reading accepted wrongly — it is ordinary by construction (T0, T1a) and worth at most a +2 lever (12.14.13; class i); a complaint misunderstood — the restatement shows it at once (class ii). *Evidence:* ROUND3-ANALYSIS S3: the code pinner answered "vitality 18" twice to a report about a purse, and other reports got "logged" or "say which fact".
cards.body:
**12.3.6 Disputes: the player's report.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` [DL-12-04; DL-12-84; DL-12-85; DL-12-86; DL-12-94; C:P13; R5 DM-08; revision: I-065; revision: R2-G; revision: R2-H]
Checking less (12.3.1b) lets some errors through on purpose; the player's report is how they are caught. The
player may say the game erred, or ask why it ruled as it did, at any time. The report is **understood first, then
verified** against evidence, never memory (PR-12-11) [revision: R2-H; DL-12-94].
1. **Reporting.** `/fix <what is wrong>` (12.5.10) is a DISPUTE by code, with no classification. A natural dispute
   ("that's wrong", "she already told me her name", "that's not what I meant", "I had two torches", "why didn't the
   success give me the purse?") is classified DISPUTE by 12.2.2. A fiction message that may also be one is handled as
   fiction, and its response ends with the fix hint. The hint, `Something wrong? Type /fix and say what.`, is also
   shown at session start (12.5.2) and in the glossary (14.2.7).
2. **Categories** (closed; from the understanding call, checked by code against what the passage is):
   `remembered_wrong` (a fact or a name), `rule_wrong` (a gate, DC, modifier, cost or odds), `contradiction` (the
   narration contradicted an earlier turn), `misread` (the Reader got the intent wrong), `ruling_question` (why a
   ruling came out as it did) [revision: R2-H], `other`.
3. **Understand first, then verify.** `[J:enum]` then `[D]`. One model call reads the report **with the whole
   transcript** (past `feedback.understand_call.transcript_budget_tokens`, the scene cards plus search hits for the
   report's words) and returns `{believes, happened, category, turn, quote}`. Real reports are fuzzy ("the season is
   wrong", "I never got the purse"), so code never pins one first by a number or a name in it; the answer restates
   the complaint back to the player in plain words. Code then verifies against the evidence: the **whole
   transcript** (every turn of the campaign, not just the scene); each stored fact's provenance (its source event,
   source kind and turn); the frame with its cited facts, its rule ids, its typed intended change (01.2.7) and the
   inputs it was computed from; the claim log.
4. **Outcomes** (by PR-12-11's table), each delivered as a **plain answer**, never "logged" alone: corrected ("You're
   right, fixed: …"), explained ("Here's why: the lift succeeded at reach 1, so …"), or not found ("I can't find
   that; did you mean …?"). **Bias: act on fiction, explain on mechanics** (INV-9):
   - **Correct**: a superseding write with `source: correction` citing the dispute, **pinned**: never archived,
     and shown in its subject's profile whenever the subject is in view (12.2.4); a record error by 12.3.4.
   - **Take back and redo the beat**: by 12.5.8, within the scene, or past its start under 12.5.8's take-back
     limit when the evidence is code-confirmed and nothing irreversible followed.
   - **Explain**: when the evidence shows the player is mistaken, or asks why a ruling stands, answer OOF with the
     turn and its words, or the stored fact and its provenance, or the frame's reasons ("Turn 22: 'She turns away
     without answering.' Her name was never given."). Nothing is written.
   - **The player's reading wins** when the evidence is uncertain and the matter is incidental fiction (T0 or T1a:
     a detail, an incidental act, an ordinary property, who said what in passing): the reading is accepted as an
     Oracle "Certain" (00.6.7) and written as a pinned correction. **INV-9 still holds for mechanics and
     consequential content** (a quantity, harm, a condition, a relevant possession, a coarse position, a clue, a
     sealed fact, a ruling): there only the record decides, and an uncertain report is answered with the evidence
     and the reason, and logged for review.
5. **Ruling disputes and questions** (`rule_wrong`, `ruling_question`): code recomputes the frame (gate, DC,
   modifiers, cost, odds, the typed change and its reach) from the rules data and the facts as they stood at its
   commit. A different result, or an established fact that changes the tier, stakes, reach or a lever and was omitted
   (`[J:flag]` *"Was an established fact that changes the tier, stakes, reach or a lever omitted from a committed
   frame?"*), is a ruling error, handled as 12.3.4 with reliance true for that beat; otherwise the ruling stands,
   explained in plain words with its rule ids and cited facts.
6. **Review log** `[D]`: every report is a dispute record `{id, time, turn, words, believes, category, passage,
   evidence (turn quotes, fact ids with provenance, frame and rule ids), outcome, writes, reverted}` in the
   corrections ledger, and an entry in the save's review log (`saves/<campaign>.disputes.md`, one block per dispute,
   newest last), written for the owner to read. **Disputes per 100 narrated turns** (all, upheld, by category) is a
   quality metric (`pacing.yaml#feedback`; OEQ-12-24), and the understanding call is tested on the real complaint
   corpus, the `/fix` lines of the persona runs, beside planted cases (OEQ-12-26).
*Worst case (J):* a valid report rejected — it stays in the review log with the player's words and the evidence,
and the player can report it again with the turn (class iv); an incidental reading accepted wrongly — it is
ordinary by construction (T0, T1a) and worth at most a +2 lever (12.14.13; class i); a complaint misunderstood — the
restatement shows it at once (class ii). *Evidence:* ROUND3-ANALYSIS S3: the code pinner answered "vitality 18" twice
to a report about a purse, and other reports got "logged" or "say which fact".

cards.title: Moderation is not consistency
cards.body:
**12.3.7 Moderation is not consistency.** `[D]` Safety removals (12.5.6–12.5.7) change *content*, are
logged separately from corrections, and never count as errors; consistency corrections change *truth*
and never invoke safety. The two tolerate different error rates — a needless safety removal costs a line
of fiction, a needless "correction" corrupts the world — and are kept in separate ledgers [C:P13; R1 12.D].

cards.title: Scenes: framing, cutting, and time modes
cards.body: ### 12.4 Scenes: framing, cutting, and time modes

cards.title: The scene record
cards.body:
**12.4.1 The scene record.** `[D]` A scene (00.18: a continuous situation with one focus) is an entity of
kind `object` with id `scn.*`, written at `scene_start`: `{id, agenda (one question), expected (the
player's expected scene, one line, or null), test_result (expected|altered|interrupted|untested), mode,
place, cast_present [ids], pillar, challenge_type, started_at, ended_at, frames [ids], intensity_points,
control_points, chaos_points}`. The **agenda** is the one question the scene exists to answer ("Does
Wren get across the river before the riders arrive?"; "What does the ferryman know?") — the Alexandrian's
scene agenda [R: https://thealexandrian.net/wordpress/31509/roleplaying-games/the-art-of-pacing]. The
agenda is written in neutral terms and never promises an answer.

cards.title: When a scene starts and when it is cut
cards.worst_case: an agenda judged answered too early cuts a scene the player wanted to continue — the player may stay ("I'm not done here"), which re-opens it with the same id (class iv).
cards.body:
**12.4.2 When a scene starts and when it is cut.** `[T]` + `[J:flag]` A scene **ends** (`mark_boundary(scene_end)`)
when the first of these is true; the next scene starts at once (`scene_start`):
1. **Agenda answered** `[J:flag]` — the scene's question now has an answer in state (a frame's degree
   settled it, a clock completed, the NPC refused or agreed). True only when a write this turn settles it.
2. **Place change** — the PC moves to a different place node (00.6.2 Place), or `travel` mode begins.
3. **Time jump** — the player skips time (`advance_time` of at least one `hour`, or any watch, day or
   downtime span), or a rest of any type completes.
4. **Interrupt** — `advance_time` halted on an interrupting handler (00.7.8): a new scene is framed at the
   interrupting moment.
5. **Conflict ends** (`conflict_end`).
6. **The player cuts** — the player says to move on ("skip ahead", "I leave", "next morning").
7. **Dead air** — `[D]` two consecutive DM turns in which the player's message held only SPEECH or free
   activities and nothing was written except time (`pacing.yaml#scenes.dead_air_turns: 2`): the DM offers
   a cut OOF in one line ("Move on to …? Or stay a while.") and frames the next scene unless the player
   stays. This is the Alexandrian's "skip empty time" made a counter [R1 M-41].
A conflict is always its own scene. *Worst case (J, 1):* an agenda judged answered too early cuts a scene
the player wanted to continue — the player may stay ("I'm not done here"), which re-opens it with the
same id (class iv).

cards.title: Framing a scene
cards.worst_case: a weaker impetus chosen from the list — the scene opens flatter, never falser (no state effect; class i in pacing terms). *Strong start:* the first scene of every session opens in medias res or at the threshold of something that demands a choice (12.5.2) [R: https://slyflourish.com/eight_steps_2023.html]. *Examples:* inside "in medias res": the PC declared "I ride for the ford before the riders catch me" — open with hooves on the far bank and the water at the stirrups, not with the ride there. Outside: "I walk into the Drowned Lantern to find the ferryman" — at the threshold (new place, social
cards.body:
**12.4.3 Framing a scene.** `[J:enum]` + `[N]` Every scene opening has four parts, in this order, in at
most **200 words** (`pacing.yaml#narration.scene_open_max_words`):
1. **The moment** — where, when (time of day and weather from state, never invented), who is present
   (each addressable element written on mention, 00.6.6), and the layout the PC can see: exits, cover,
   hazards, what is within reach (12.14.6). A seeded place's look, furniture and exits (12.16.9) are this layout,
   read from the store and never invented [revision: R2-D; I-130], and given here once (12.14.11, setting once)
   [revision: R2-I; DL-12-99].
2. **The impetus** — one thing that is happening or about to, drawn `[J:enum]` from this ordered list,
   first eligible: (a) the scene test's alteration or interruption (12.4.4); (b) a fired trigger
   (12.2.3); (c) the PC's own declared purpose for the scene; (d) an NPC present acting on a recorded
   want; (e) a sensed or hidden clock's latest omen; (f) the most overdue rotation axis's opportunity
   (12.9.2). The impetus comes from state; it is never invented to be dramatic.
3. **Framing hardness** `[J:enum]`: **in medias res** (start at the first moment of decision or danger —
   default for interrupts, chases, ambushes, and any scene whose approach holds no decision); **at the
   threshold** (start as the PC arrives — default for new places and social scenes); **open** (start
   with the PC at leisure — only for downtime and havens). Default when uncertain: at the threshold.
   Skip any stretch in which no meaningful decision could be made
   [R: https://thealexandrian.net/wordpress/31520/roleplaying-games/the-art-of-pacing-part-2-scene-framing;
   R1 M-41]. **Travel** between places frames the arrival [revision: R2-I; DL-12-98]: a scene that opens because
   the PC went somewhere opens at the threshold with the arrival narrated (the road's end, the gate, the door and what
   is through it), never with a bare "It works." or a jump with no travel (P-098).
4. **The open prompt** (12.14.9).
*Narration may not imply:* any element not written on mention; any clock fill not public; a sealed fact.
*Worst case (J):* a weaker impetus chosen from the list — the scene opens flatter, never falser (no state
effect; class i in pacing terms). *Strong start:* the first scene of every session opens in medias res
or at the threshold of something that demands a choice (12.5.2) [R: https://slyflourish.com/eight_steps_2023.html].
*Examples:* inside "in medias res": the PC declared "I ride for the ford before the riders catch me" —
open with hooves on the far bank and the water at the stirrups, not with the ride there. Outside: "I
walk into the Drowned Lantern to find the ferryman" — at the threshold (new place, social). Non-example:
opening a downtime week at the monastery in medias res with an invented fire — the impetus list has no
fire in it unless a roll or clock put one there.

cards.title: The scene test
cards.worst_case: a less likely version of the altered scene chosen — one person or object different, written as fact, never harmful by itself (class i). [R5 P-05; R6 B-16]
cards.body:
**12.4.4 The scene test.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` At every `scene_start`, handler `h.12.scene_test` (phase 7)
runs the test unless the scene is **untested**: a direct continuation (same place, less than one
interval later), a conflict, an interrupt's own scene, or a scene the player framed as downtime in a
haven. Otherwise:
1. The DM writes the **expected scene** in one line from the player's stated plan ("Wren reaches the
   ferry landing at dusk and finds the ferryman").
2. The engine rolls `tbl.scene_test` (d10). With **tension** T (12.6.3), the scene **deviates** when the
   roll ≤ T − 3: an **odd** roll → **altered**, an **even** roll → **interrupted**; otherwise **expected**.
3. **Altered**: `roll_table(tbl.scene_adjustment)` → one adjustment (add or remove a person; intensify or
   reduce an activity; add or remove an object; shift the time; change a feature of the place; two
   adjustments; someone already here for the same reason [verification: V2b-015]). The DM applies it as the next most likely version of the expected scene `[J:enum]`
   (which person, which object — from state or a table), and writes it.
4. **Interrupted**: a random event replaces the expected scene (12.6.5); the expected scene is still
   available afterwards if the player pursues it.
Deviation rates by tension (T-12-9): T 1–3 none; T 4 10% (altered only); T 5 20%; T 6 30%; T 7 40%;
T 8 50%; T 9 60%; altered and interrupted split as odd and even faces.
*Why lower than Mythic.* Mythic's test deviates whenever d10 ≤ Chaos (50% at the default 5) because in
Mythic the scene test and random events are the world's *only* motion [R5 P-05]. Here the world already
moves through clocks, watch and interval checks, the World Turn and NPC wants, so the scene test is a
seasoning, not the engine: 20% at the default tension, rising to 60% when the PC has lost control
[DL-12-06]. *Worst case (J):* a less likely version of the altered scene chosen — one person or object
different, written as fact, never harmful by itself (class i). [R5 P-05; R6 B-16]

cards.title: Time modes and transitions
cards.body:
**12.4.5 Time modes and transitions.** `[D]` + `[J:enum]` [DL-12-01; R5 TM-03; revision: I-065] At every `scene_start` the DM classifies the mode
(00.7.3; default the previous scene's; uncertain → `free`). Within a scene, the mode changes only on the
transitions of T-12-3, each of which calls `mark_boundary(mode_change)`; handler `h.12.mode_change`
loads the new mode's cards (by the `situation.*` tags listed in T-12-3) and sets time-per-beat.

cards.title: Mode transitions
cards.worst_case: the mode classified wrongly at a scene start — time per beat is wrong for at most that scene; site danger clocks still tick from costs (class i, 00.7.3).
cards.body:
**T-12-3 Mode transitions** (canonical: `pacing.yaml#modes`).

| From → to | Fires when (closed list) | Cards loaded |
|---|---|---|
| any → `conflict` | an adversary's behavior list attacks; the PC declares a Strike, Grapple or harmful Force or ability against a creature that resists; a hostile NPC action result says "attacks"; a clock completion creates an attacking encounter (`conflict_start`, 06.2.1) [revision: I-030] | `situation.conflict.*` |
| `conflict` → previous | `conflict_end` (06.13.1): no hostile participant able and willing to act, a side's objective met, a truce, or the PC gone or defeated [revision: I-030] | the previous mode's |
| any → `site` | the PC enters a place tagged as a site (ch.10) or begins a room-by-room search of a building | `situation.exploration.*` |
| any → `travel` | the PC departs along a route link between places (ch.10) | `situation.travel.*` |
| any → `downtime` | in a haven, the player declares a downtime activity (ch.15) or a span of days | `situation.downtime.*` |
| any → `free` | the PC leaves a site for a settlement place, arrives from travel, ends downtime, or none of the above applies | `situation.social.*`, `situation.investigation.*` by scene tags |

*Worst case (J):* the mode classified wrongly at a scene start — time per beat is wrong for at most that
scene; site danger clocks still tick from costs (class i, 00.7.3).

cards.title: Skipping time
cards.body:
**12.4.6 Skipping time.** `[D]` When the player skips time ("we travel three days", "I spend the winter at
the monastery") the DM calls `advance_time` and narrates *only from the returned list* of boundaries,
omens, rumors, handler results and interrupts, in chronological order, at most one sentence per
returned item and at most **150 words** for the whole skip unless an interrupt frames a new scene
(`pacing.yaml#narration.skip_max_words`). It invents no weather, encounter, rumor or change that is not in
the list (PR-00-2 step 5). If the skip halts on an interrupt, the remainder is offered back to the
player after the interrupting scene (00.7.8) [R5 TM-10; 00.7.7].

cards.title: Montage
cards.body:
**12.4.7 Montage.** `[D]` A montage is a time skip with repeated activity ("I spend the week asking around
the docks"). It is resolved as ch.15's or ch.10's activity for its listed duration, with one frame per
activity unit as those chapters set, run inside `advance_time`. The narration is the skip narration of
12.4.6 plus each frame's result in one sentence. No montage compresses rolls (01.2.3; 01.14.3)
[R: https://thealexandrian.net/wordpress/44117/roleplaying-games/scenario-structure-challenge-5-the-rpg-montage].

cards.title: Scene-end bookkeeping
cards.body:
**12.4.8 Scene-end bookkeeping.** `[D]` Handler `h.12.bookkeeping` (`scene_end`, phase 9; mirrored on
`session_end`, 00.7.9) runs, in order (Mythic's end-of-scene adjustments made explicit [R5 P-09]):
1. **Tension** update (12.6.3) — `h.12.tension_update`.
2. **Intensity and phase** update (12.7.2) — `h.12.intensity_scene` (contrib handler).
3. **Lists**: the cast list and thread list weights are updated (12.6.6).
4. **Sweep**: every trigger raised during the scene was handled (12.2.3); every hidden or sensed clock
   tick rendered one omen (INV-14); every claim of class `position`, `possession`, `quantity` and
   `harm_condition` in the scene's delivered narration, each declared sentence's claims as well as those the
   audit found (12.3.1) [revision: R2-E], is re-checked against the store with
   `check_claims`, narrator voice and certain subjects only (12.3.1b) [revision: R2-G] — a mismatch found here
   starts PR-12-4.
5. **Live-lead audit** (12.8.4) — `h.12.lead_audit` (contrib handler).
6. **Rotation ledger** (12.9.1) — `h.12.rotation_update` (contrib handler).
7. **NPC memory** commit (12.11.7) — `h.12.npc_memory` (contrib handler).
8. **Scene details expire** [revision: R2-E; DL-12-72]: every `scene` detail (00.6.6a) and every activity written
   for the scene (12.11.9) is superseded at `ended_at`; history is kept. Range bands between people (06.3.2) are
   cleared then too: a band from one scene's scuffle never carries into the next [revision: R2-F].
9. **Scene card** [revision: R2-E; DL-12-73]: a structured view over the scene's events, never a summary of its
   narration: `{scene, place, time (started_at, ended_at), cast, agenda -> answer, beats [(actor, verb, target,
   degree)], facts written, memories committed (step 7), threads touched}`. Every field is computed from the
   log, so the card can be regenerated at any time and is never summarized again (00.6.9d); it holds no prose,
   and each role reads it through its view (12.2.4).
